dart2js compile time vs. generated code shape

2026-10-02T06:46:14.899304 · Dart 3.14.0-edge.049a4035b0ac3ac49c5199b0319b164e17b3fa3d · macos Version 27.0.1 (Build 26A434) · 10 cores · 259 compiles, N = 1 to 4000

Each point is a single dart compile js -O3 --csp of a generated program with N classes, all instantiated in one main. Variants change one aspect of the generated code; see variants in gen.dart.

Comparing variants: Synthetic ZBase_i classes

Each ZBase_i has an int field plus some combination of ==, hashCode and toString overrides.

  • The parameter type of == makes no meaningful difference: == (dynamic other), == (Object other) and == (Object? other) are within 4.5% of each other at N=4000, which is within the run-to-run noise of a single compile.
  • Overriding == costs 1.58s (1.5×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 4.88s vs. no == override at 3.29s). The biggest difference is in Type inference (285ms, 18% of it). Scaling goes from N0.85 to N0.89.
  • Adding a hashCode override to a toString override costs 1.12s (1.5×) at N=4000 (no == override at 3.29s vs. toString only at 2.17s). The biggest difference is in kernel loader (215ms, 19% of it). Scaling goes from N0.74 to N0.85.
  • Adding a toString override to a hashCode override costs 736ms (1.3×) at N=4000 (no == override at 3.29s vs. hashCode only at 2.56s). The biggest difference is in Code emitter (158ms, 21% of it), mostly source-maps (108ms). Scaling goes from N0.81 to N0.85.
  • Reading the shared field val inside toString costs 256ms (1.1×) at N=4000 (toString only at 2.17s vs. toString only, no field read at 1.92s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (70ms, 27% of it). Scaling goes from N0.74 to N0.74.
  • A toString override that does not read any field costs 462ms (1.3×) at N=4000 (toString only, no field read at 1.92s vs. no overrides at 1.45s). The biggest difference is in SSA optimizer (99ms, 21% of it). Scaling goes from N0.68 to N0.74.
  • Every class declaring a field with the same name (vs. unique names) makes little difference at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 4.88s vs. == (dynamic other), unique field names at 4.71s). Scaling goes from N0.90 to N0.89.
  • Declaring val on every subclass (vs. once on the base class) costs 415ms (1.1×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 4.88s vs. == (dynamic other), field on base class at 4.46s). The biggest difference is in Front end (121ms, 29% of it), mostly worldImpact (83ms). Scaling goes from N0.89 to N0.89.
  • All N inserts in one giant main (vs. helpers of 100 statements) makes little difference at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 4.88s vs. == (dynamic other), main split up at 4.66s). Scaling goes from N0.86 to N0.89.
  • A giant main once field names are unique makes little difference at N=4000 (== (dynamic other), unique field names at 4.71s vs. unique field names + main split up at 4.80s). Scaling goes from N0.87 to N0.90.
  • All classes in one library (vs. a library per class, same public field name) saves 1.58s (1.3×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 4.88s vs. == (dynamic other), library per class at 6.46s). The biggest difference is in kernel loader (1.11s, 70% of it). Scaling goes from N0.87 to N0.89.
  • A public field name shared across libraries (vs. a private _val per library) saves 678ms (1.1×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other), library per class at 6.46s vs. == (dynamic other), library per class, private _val at 7.14s). The biggest difference is in Code emitter (629ms, 93% of it), mostly write fragments (353ms). Scaling goes from N0.90 to N0.87.

Comparing variants: Frugal-style structs

Each N adds one struct shaped like Frugal’s generated Dart (six fields whose names id, name, description, count, tags and child are shared by every struct; child is the previous struct), in its own library, plus a service client calling through FMethod. So N=1000 is 2000 classes. The variants apply the generator changes recommended in research/frugal-dart-codegen.md. These stop at N=1000 because they are much slower to compile.

  • Generated internals going through the shared public getters, isSetX() and validate() (vs. private fields and _validate()) costs 2.56s (1.1×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 22.9s vs. Frugal-style, internals use private fields and _validate() at 20.3s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (796ms, 31% of it). Scaling goes from N0.98 to N1.02.
  • FMethod calling Function.apply on a tear-off (vs. a typed closure) makes little difference at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 22.9s vs. Frugal-style, FMethod without Function.apply at 22.6s). Scaling goes from N1.00 to N1.02.
  • static final descriptors, implicit dynamic return types and a new DeepCollectionEquality per call (vs. const, explicit types and a shared instance) costs 1.65s (1.1×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 22.9s vs. Frugal-style, const descriptors and explicit return types at 21.2s). The biggest difference is in Code emitter (330ms, 20% of it). Scaling goes from N1.00 to N1.02.
  • Generating getFieldValue, setFieldValue, isSet, clone and toString (vs. a lean mode without them) costs 7.55s (1.5×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 22.9s vs. Frugal-style, no getFieldValue/setFieldValue/isSet/clone/toString at 15.3s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (2.23s, 29% of it). Scaling goes from N0.99 to N1.02.
  • Inline list loops in read/write (vs. shared runtime helpers) makes little difference at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 22.9s vs. Frugal-style, shared list read/write helpers at 22.3s). Scaling goes from N1.02 to N1.02.
  • Frugal output as generated today (vs. all recommended changes together) costs 9.80s (1.8×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 22.9s vs. Frugal-style, all of the above at 13.1s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (2.79s, 29% of it). Scaling goes from N0.99 to N1.02.

Breakdown for == (dynamic other)

  • Compile time went from 427ms at N=1 to 4.88s at N=4000, 11× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N0.89 (about linear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from SSA optimizer (+714ms, 16% of the increase), Code emitter (+700ms, 16% of the increase) and Type inference (+613ms, 14% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: SSA optimizer (N1.09, 15% of the time), Front end (N1.07, 7.6% of the time) and Code emitter (N1.03, 15% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=4000, SSA optimizer grew from 7.4% to 15% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 34% to 15%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows as roughly N0.96 (about 41 inferred types per class), in line with compile time. The slowdown is mostly explained by there being more code, not by a per-item cost that grows.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 145ms of wall-clock time on average.

Total compile time

Where the time goes

Top-level dart2js phases stacked, so the top edge is the total compile time.

Scaling on a log-log scale

On log-log axes a phase growing as Nk is a straight line with slope k. Lines steeper than the total are taking a growing share of compile time.

Largest sub-phases

Phase breakdown

"Share of increase" is how much of the total slowdown from N=1 to N=4000 the phase accounts for. "Scaling" is the exponent k of a power-law fit t ≈ a·Nk over runs with N ≥ 1000 (1 is linear, 2 is quadratic). Sub-phases under 5 ms are hidden.

Breakdown for == (Object other)

  • Compile time went from 331ms at N=1 to 4.70s at N=4000, 14× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N0.89 (about linear).

  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: Code emitter > write fragments (N1.07, 5.3% of the time), SSA optimizer (N1.03, 16% of the time) and Code emitter (N1.01, 15% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.

  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows as roughly N0.96 (about 41 inferred types per class), in line with compile time. The slowdown is mostly explained by there being more code, not by a per-item cost that grows.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 93ms of wall-clock time on average.

  • Compile time went from 337ms at N=1 to 1.92s at N=4000, 5.7× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N0.74 (sublinear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from kernel loader (+311ms, 20% of the increase), SSA optimizer (+285ms, 18% of the increase) and Code emitter (+264ms, 17% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: SSA optimizer (N1.15, 16% of the time), Code emitter > build program (N1.05, 5.1% of the time) and Code emitter (N0.97, 15% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.

  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows as roughly N0.93 (about 10 inferred types per class), in line with compile time. The slowdown is mostly explained by there being more code, not by a per-item cost that grows.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 93ms of wall-clock time on average.

Breakdown for Frugal-style, all of the above

  • Compile time went from 428ms at N=1 to 13.1s at N=1000, 31× slower for 1000× more classes. From N=250 up it scales as roughly N0.99 (about linear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from kernel loader (+2.08s, 16% of the increase), Type inference (+2.07s, 16% of the increase) and Code emitter (+1.87s, 15% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=1000: Enqueue (N1.11, 5.4% of the time), self (N1.10, 8.6% of the time) and Code emitter (N1.02, 15% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=1000, Type inference grew from 15% to 16% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 23% to 17%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows as roughly N0.96 (about 639 inferred types per class), in line with compile time. The slowdown is mostly explained by there being more code, not by a per-item cost that grows.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 93ms of wall-clock time on average.
